screens.title: Integrating Native Modules & Device Features
screens.subtitle: How the React Native Bridge, built-in APIs, and native modules let JavaScript access device capabilities

narration.text: In this chapter we will explore how React Native lets your JavaScript code reach into platform APIs and device features. You will learn what the React Native bridge is, why it exists, and when to use built-in JavaScript modules like PermissionsAndroid versus third-party libraries or custom native modules. We will walk through concrete examples for requesting runtime permissions on Android and show the manifest entries that must accompany those requests. You will also learn the basic pattern for creating a native module on Android — the class, the @ReactMethod annotation, and registering the module — so you have a mental model even if you don’t write native code yet. Finally, we’ll discuss common mistakes such as forgetting AndroidManifest entries, incorrect linking, and version mismatches, and how to handle permission denials gracefully in your UI. By the end, you’ll understand the trade-offs: built-in APIs are quick, third-party libraries cover many cases, and custom native modules are the escape hatch when nothing else fits. Consider where your app needs native performance or access, and keep user privacy and permission UX at the center of your design.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: The React Native Bridge connects JavaScript and native platform code, enabling access to device features while giving you choices: built-in APIs for common tasks, third-party libraries for feature coverage, and custom native modules when you need platform-specific control.

Understand the bridge between JavaScript and native code, practice Android permission requests, and learn when to use libraries or author native modules.

Why this matters

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll build and evidence of competency

narration.text: These learning objectives map to practical skills you will use when integrating device features. First, you will understand the concept of the React Native bridge — what it does and why it is necessary — and be able to explain, with an example, how JavaScript can call native Android or iOS code. Second, you will be able to use common built-in React Native APIs for device features, such as PermissionsAndroid on Android, and demonstrate requesting and handling permission results in an app. Third, you will learn how to evaluate and use third-party libraries that wrap native functionality, understanding the trade-offs between using Expo-managed libraries versus linking native modules in a CLI project. Fourth, you will be familiar with the process for creating a custom native module at a high level: declare a module class, annotate methods to expose them to JavaScript, and register the module so JavaScript can import it. Each objective includes a milestone so you can verify competency by implementing a small permission flow or describing the native module registration process.

screens.title: The React Native Bridge
screens.subtitle: What the bridge is and why it enables native access

narration.text: The React Native bridge is the communication layer that allows JavaScript code to invoke methods in platform-specific native modules and for native code to send events back to JavaScript. At a high level, JavaScript runs in an engine such as Hermes or JavaScriptCore and communicates across the bridge with messages that reach native modules implemented in Kotlin/Java on Android or Swift/Objective-C on iOS. This is essential because not every platform A P I is exposed to JavaScript, and some performance-critical features are best implemented natively. A concrete example is requesting camera access: JavaScript calls a built-in module like PermissionsAndroid. request and the bridge ensures the native Android permission dialog is shown and the result is returned as a promise. A common misconception is to think the bridge automatically makes all native APIs available; it does not. Only the methods explicitly exposed by native modules are reachable. Another misconception is believing this is a synchronous direct function call. In practice the bridge typically marshals messages and results, often asynchronously, so you'll work with Promises or callbacks. Key takeaway: the bridge is the escape hatch and integration point — use built-in modules first, then community libraries, and finally custom modules when necessary. How would you explain when to reach for a custom native module versus a library in your next app?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A messaging layer that connects the JavaScript runtime to native platform code so JS can call native functionality and receive results.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › The React Native Bridge
Core Concept

Bridge: message-based communication

The bridge marshals calls between JS engines like Hermes and platform-native modules. Calls are asynchronous, so Promises and callbacks are the usual pattern.

Example
Request camera permission using a built-in module. JavaScript requests, the native dialog appears, then the result resolves a Promise back in JS.
Common misconception
The bridge does not expose arbitrary native APIs automatically; only methods explicitly exposed by native modules can be called.
Annotated call flow
JavaScript Engine → Bridge → Native Module → Platform API → Bridge → JavaScript
JS code calls request() and returns a Promise.
Bridge serializes the message and forwards it to native code.
Native module runs platform API, e.g., show system permission dialog.
Native returns result to JS via bridge; Promise resolves.
Key Takeaway

The bridge is the controlled channel for JS-native interaction; design calls thoughtfully and prefer existing modules where possible.

screens.title: Using PermissionsAndroid (Camera example)
screens.subtitle: A worked example of requesting and handling camera permission on Android

narration.text: PermissionsAndroid is a built-in React Native A P I that provides a JavaScript interface for requesting Android runtime permissions. The common pattern is to call PermissionsAndroid. request with the permission constant, a title and message for the permission dialog, and await the returned value. In the camera example shown on screen, the component keeps a permission status in state and updates it depending on whether PermissionsAndroid. RESULTS. GRANTED is returned. If granted, you can proceed to access the camera; if denied, you should handle the denied state gracefully by disabling camera-dependent UI or offering an alternative. A common mistake is assuming the manifest declaration alone is sufficient; you must both declare the permission in AndroidManifest. xml and request it at runtime for dangerous permissions. Another pitfall is not handling errors from the request call; include a try/catch and update UI to show an error state. As a practical reflection: test both accept and deny flows on an emulator to ensure your UI remains clear and informative when users choose not to grant access. Using PermissionsAndroid (Camera example) means call permissionsandroid.request with permission constants and handle results.granted or denied states; always declare permissions in androidmanifest.xml too.. In practical terms, a worked example of requesting and handling camera permission on android. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pattern
keyIdea.text: Call PermissionsAndroid.request with permission constants and handle RESULTS.GRANTED or denied states; always declare permissions in AndroidManifest.xml too.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › PermissionsAndroid Walkthrough
Process

Request camera permission

Follow the request-await-check pattern and update UI state depending on RESULTS.GRANTED or other values.

Concrete example
<!-- JavaScript snippet -->
import React, { useState } from 'react';
import { View, Text, Button, PermissionsAndroid, Alert, StyleSheet } from 'react-native';

export default function PermissionRequester() {
  const [cameraPermissionStatus, setCameraPermissionStatus] = useState('unknown');

  const requestCameraPermission = async () => {
    try {
      const granted = await PermissionsAndroid.request(
        PermissionsAndroid.PERMISSIONS.CAMERA,
        {
          title: "Camera Permission",
          message: "This app needs access to your camera to take photos.",
          buttonNeutral: "Ask Me Later",
          buttonNegative: "Cancel",
          buttonPositive: "OK"
        }
      );
      if (granted === PermissionsAndroid.RESULTS.GRANTED) {
        setCameraPermissionStatus('granted');
        Alert.alert("Permission Granted", "You can now use the camera!");
      } else {
        setCameraPermissionStatus('denied');
        Alert.alert("Permission Denied", "Camera access was denied.");
      }
    } catch (err) {
      console.warn(err);
      setCameraPermissionStatus('error');
    }
  };
}
Explanation & checks
  • Always declare <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.CAMERA" /> in AndroidManifest.xml.
  • Handle RESULTS.GRANTED and other values; update the UI so users understand the app state.
  • Wrap requests in try/catch to catch errors and set an explicit error state.
  • Test grant and deny flows to confirm graceful degradation when permission is denied.
Key Takeaway

Permission requests are asynchronous and require both manifest declaration and runtime user consent; handle all states cleanly in your UI.

screens.title: AndroidManifest.xml and Permissions
screens.subtitle: Why manifest entries are required and what to declare

narration.text: Android requires you to declare certain permissions in AndroidManifest. xml so the system knows what your app may request. Declaring a permission in the manifest is necessary but not sufficient for dangerous permissions; you also need to request them at runtime using PermissionsAndroid. request. For example, to request camera permission you must add to your manifest. For location services, add ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION and ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION as shown in the hands-on activity. A common error is believing the manifest declaration automatically grants the permission; it does not. The manifest only signals intent and allows the system to display the runtime permission dialog. When building or testing, ensure your manifest lives in the correct path (android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest. xml) and that you rebuild the app after changing manifest entries. If a permission-dependent feature silently fails, first check the manifest, then verify runtime checks with PermissionsAndroid. check, and finally request the permission if needed. The core practice is: declare permissions, check current status, then request and handle the result. AndroidManifest.xml and Permissions means declare required permissions in androidmanifest.xml and always perform runtime checks and requests for dangerous permissions.. In practical terms, why manifest entries are required and what to declare. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Manifest rule
keyIdea.text: Declare required permissions in AndroidManifest.xml and always perform runtime checks and requests for dangerous permissions.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › AndroidManifest & Permissions
Manifest declaration example
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.CAMERA" />

<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION" />
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION" />
Place these lines in android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml and rebuild your app after changes.
Checklist when permissions fail
  • Confirm manifest entries exist in the correct manifest file path.
  • Use PermissionsAndroid.check to see current status before requesting.
  • Request at runtime and handle RESULTS.GRANTED, denied, and errors.
  • Rebuild the native app after changing manifest entries, especially on Android.
Pro tip

When testing, simulate both acceptance and denial flows so your app degrades gracefully if the user refuses a permission.

screens.title: Built-in APIs vs Third-Party Libraries
screens.subtitle: Choosing between provided modules and community packages

narration.text: When you need device functionality, you have three main options: use built-in React Native modules, adopt a third-party library, or write a custom native module. Built-in modules, like PermissionsAndroid, are convenient and maintained by the core project; they’re often the simplest path for common tasks. Third-party libraries wrap native capabilities—examples include react-native-camera or expo-camera for camera access, and react-native-geolocation-service or expo-location for location. These libraries can provide feature-rich APIs but may require installation steps and linking. The choice frequently hinges on your project setup: Expo-managed workflows often provide pre-linked expo-* libraries that require minimal work, while React Native CLI projects may rely on auto-linking or manual native linking depending on versions. A common misconception is that third-party libraries always require manual linking; newer React Native versions commonly auto-link modules, but you should consult the library documentation. Another point is maintenance: community libraries vary in upkeep and compatibility; always verify version compatibility with your React Native version. In practice, begin with built-in APIs, then use a well-maintained third-party library if you need more features, and reserve custom native modules for specialized performance or platform-specific requirements.

keyIdea.title: Decision guide
keyIdea.text: Use built-ins for common tasks, third-party libraries for richer features, and custom native modules only when necessary for performance or missing capabilities.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Built-in vs Third-Party
Built-in modules
Examples: PermissionsAndroid. Pros: stable, minimal install effort. Cons: limited feature surface for advanced device integration.
When to use
  • Simple permission checks or system dialogs.
  • When cross-platform parity is available.
Third-party libraries
Examples: react-native-camera, expo-camera, react-native-geolocation-service, expo-location. Pros: richer APIs and device features. Cons: installation, linking, and maintenance considerations.
Consider
  • Whether you use Expo managed workflow or React Native CLI.
  • Library compatibility and auto-linking support in your React Native version.
Quick checklist before adding a library
Check compatibility
Read install steps
Test grant/deny flows
If a library lacks features or has breaking incompatibilities, plan for a custom native module or another maintained alternative.

screens.title: Creating a Custom Native Module (Android overview)
screens.subtitle: High-level steps to expose native functionality to JavaScript

narration.text: When an existing A P I or library does not meet your needs, you can create a custom native module. The chapter outlines three essential steps for Android. Step one: create a native module class that extends ReactContextBaseJavaModule and implement getName to provide a module identifier that JavaScript will use. Step two: annotate methods you want to expose to JavaScript with @ReactMethod; these methods can accept arguments and return results via callbacks or Promises. Step three: register your module by adding it to your package so React Native can discover it, typically in MainApplication. java or MainApplication. kt where packages are listed. A concrete example is exposing a specialized image processing routine written in Kotlin to JavaScript as a Promise-based method. Common misconceptions include thinking that native methods are automatically available or that they must be synchronous — in reality, you control whether to call callbacks or resolve Promises asynchronously. Also remember to declare any platform-level permissions or services in AndroidManifest. xml if the module requires them. Use native modules sparingly: they are powerful, but add maintenance overhead and platform-specific code.

keyIdea.title: Three-step overview
keyIdea.text: Create a module class, expose methods with @ReactMethod, then register the module in your application package so JavaScript can call it.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Custom Native Module
1. Create module class
Subclass ReactContextBaseJavaModule and override getName to provide the module name that JS will import.
2. Expose methods
Annotate methods with @ReactMethod. Use callbacks or Promises to return results asynchronously.
3. Register module
Add the module to your React package in MainApplication.java or MainApplication.kt so the bridge can find it.
Example scenario
Suppose you need a custom image decoder for performance. Implement decoding in Kotlin, expose decodeImage as a @ReactMethod that returns a Promise, and register the module for use from JavaScript.
Common mistake

Forgetting to register the module or to declare required AndroidManifest entries will make the native method unreachable from JavaScript.

screens.title: Linking, Auto-linking, and Expo Differences
screens.subtitle: How libraries are connected to your native project

narration.text: Integrating third-party native libraries can involve linking steps that connect native code to your Android and iOS projects. Historically, libraries required manual linking, but newer React Native versions support auto-linking which links native modules automatically during build. If you use Expo's managed workflow, many device features are already exposed via expo-* libraries and are pre-linked, greatly simplifying installation. When using the React Native CLI or an ejected project, some libraries still need manual installation or extra native configuration; follow the library documentation carefully. A common pitfall is assuming auto-linking always resolves installation issues — sometimes additional manifest entries, Gradle changes, or native dependency configuration is required. If a library's native code is not found at runtime, verify that gradle builds include the module, check MainApplication package registrations if applicable, and rebuild the app. When choosing a library, confirm whether it supports Expo managed workflow or requires native project changes. The practical approach: prefer Expo libraries in managed apps for speed, rely on well-documented community libraries with auto-linking for CLI projects, and be prepared to add manifest or build changes for advanced native dependencies.

keyIdea.title: Linking guidance
keyIdea.text: Auto-linking reduces manual setup, Expo-managed projects come pre-linked for many features, but always check documentation for additional native configuration and manifest entries.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Linking & Expo
Auto-linking
Modern React Native versions auto-link native modules during the build, reducing manual installation steps for many libraries.
Check the library README for any additional setup steps like manifest edits or Gradle configuration.
Expo-managed workflow
Expo often provides pre-linked expo-* libraries so you can use device features with minimal native changes; this simplifies development if you stay within Expo capabilities.
If you eject from Expo, you may need to follow native install steps similar to React Native CLI projects.
Debugging linking issues
  • Rebuild the native app after changes.
  • Check that the native module appears in Gradle build output and that the package is registered.
  • Inspect the library documentation for manual steps if auto-linking didn’t cover them.

GRANTED and update state accordingly, then show an alert or UI message communicating that location services are available. Important details: test both accepted and denied responses so the UI degrades gracefully; use PermissionsAndroid. check to preflight the current state before requesting; and wrap your request in try/catch to capture any errors. A common misconception is to request all permissions at startup; instead, request permissions in context when the feature is needed so users understand the value. <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION" />

Starter App.js snippet
import React, { useState } from 'react';
import { View, Text, Button, PermissionsAndroid, Alert, StyleSheet } from 'react-native';

export default function App() {
  const [locationPermissionStatus, setLocationPermissionStatus] = useState('unknown');

  const requestLocationPermission = async () => {
    try {
      const granted = await PermissionsAndroid.request(
        PermissionsAndroid.PERMISSIONS.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION,
        {
          title: "Location Permission",
          message: "This app needs access to your location to provide personalized services.",
          buttonNeutral: "Ask Me Later",
          buttonNegative: "Cancel",
          buttonPositive: "OK"
        }
      );
      if (granted === PermissionsAndroid.RESULTS.GRANTED) {
        setLocationPermissionStatus('granted');
        Alert.alert("Permission Granted", "You can now access location services!");
      } else {
        setLocationPermissionStatus('denied');
        Alert.alert("Permission Denied", "Location access was denied.");
      }
    } catch (err) {
      console.warn(err);
      setLocationPermissionStatus('error');
    }
  };
}
Test both grant and deny flows, check status before requesting with PermissionsAndroid.check, and avoid asking permissions before the user understands why the feature needs them.

screens.title: Common Integration Mistakes & Debugging
screens.subtitle: Troubleshooting linker, manifest, and async issues

narration.text: Integrating native modules often exposes a small set of recurring mistakes. First, forgetting AndroidManifest entries is common — declare permissions, services, and activities your native code relies on. Second, incorrect linking or missed package registration can make a module unavailable at runtime; check auto-linking behavior for your React Native version and, if necessary, add manual linking steps or register the package in MainApplication. Third, version mismatches between React Native and a library can cause build failures; always consult the library documentation for compatible versions. Fourth, async/await misuse can lead to unhandled Promise rejections when calling native modules that return Promises; wrap calls in try/catch or use. then/. catch to handle errors. As a concrete debugging sequence: check your manifest entries, rebuild the app, inspect Gradle output for missing native modules, verify that the module is registered, and add logging to native code if you control it. A helpful misconception to avoid is assuming a failing native call will always surface a clear error in JavaScript; sometimes native exceptions must be inspected in native logs. The takeaway: systematic checks and clear error handling reduce integration friction and speed up resolution.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshooting steps
keyIdea.text: When integration fails, verify manifest entries, check linking/registration, confirm version compatibility, and handle Promises and errors explicitly.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Common Mistakes
Missing manifest entries
Declare permissions and any services or activities used by native code, then rebuild the app to apply changes.
Incorrect linking
Verify auto-linking output or manually register the package in MainApplication if needed.
Version mismatches
Confirm library compatibility with your React Native version to avoid build-time failures.
Async handling & errors
  • Use try/catch around async native calls and present a clear error state in the UI.
  • Check native logs when JavaScript errors are insufficient for diagnosis.
Follow a sequence: manifest, linking, compatibility, then logging for effective debugging.

screens.title: Permission UX and Safety Considerations
screens.subtitle: Request only what you need and explain why

narration.text: Permission requests affect user trust, so approach them thoughtfully. Only request permissions at the moment they are needed and explain clearly why the app requires that access. For example, if you need location to show nearby stores, prompt for location when the user opens map features and include a short explanation in the dialog message. The chapter emphasizes that over-requesting permissions can deter users and may lead to app rejections. When a user denies a permission, provide alternative functionality or a helpful explanation and avoid repeatedly prompting. Also, handle the denied state in your UI by disabling features gracefully and offering a clear path to settings if the user changes their mind. From a safety perspective, never request unnecessary permissions and minimize the scope of sensitive data collection. A good practice is to log permission-denied flows during development so you can refine messaging and minimize friction. The key takeaway: treat permission requests as a conversation with the user, not a technical formality. Permission UX and Safety Considerations means request permissions in context, explain the reason, handle denials gracefully, and avoid over-requesting to maintain user trust.. In practical terms, request only what you need and explain why. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: UX principle
keyIdea.text: Request permissions in context, explain the reason, handle denials gracefully, and avoid over-requesting to maintain user trust.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Permission UX
Contextual requests
Ask for permissions when the user takes an action that needs them, and include a clear message explaining the benefit.
Example: only request camera when the user taps "Take Photo".
Handle denial gracefully
Disable related features, show helpful messaging, and offer a pathway to app settings if necessary.
Privacy and app store risk
Request only what is necessary; unnecessary requests may result in user churn or app review issues. Make the value clear and minimize sensitive data collection.
Check your messages

Concise, honest dialog messages improve grant rates. Test and iterate on wording during development.

screens.title: When to use built-in APIs, libraries, or custom modules
screens.subtitle: A decision checklist for architects and developers

narration.text: Deciding whether to use a built-in A P I, a third-party library, or a custom native module requires balancing speed, features, maintenance, and platform needs. Start by asking: does a built-in A P I solve the problem? If yes, prefer it for stability. If not, look for a maintained third-party library that provides the needed features and has compatible versions with your React Native and native toolchain. If a library exists but requires too many native changes or lacks security guarantees, consider whether you can fork or contribute, or if writing a small custom native module is warranted. Custom native modules are appropriate when you need highly optimized code, access to platform APIs not exposed by libraries, or tight control over threading and memory. Remember maintenance cost: native modules increase platform-specific code and testing. A typical misconception is to default to custom native modules for marginal gains; prefer established libraries and only escalate to custom implementation when the benefits justify the added complexity. Before deciding, create a short evaluation checklist: functional fit, compatibility, maintenance, security, and required native changes. This ensures your choice is pragmatic and maintainable.

keyIdea.title: Decision checklist
keyIdea.text: Evaluate functional fit, compatibility, maintenance burden, and native changes required before choosing built-in APIs, third-party libraries, or custom modules.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Decision Checklist
Functional fit
Does the API/library provide the exact behavior and stability you need?
Compatibility & maintenance
Is the library actively maintained and compatible with your RN version?
Native changes required
Will using it require manifest edits, Gradle changes, or manual linking?
When to write custom native code
Only when performance, security, or missing platform APIs justify the increased maintenance cost of native modules.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: These key concepts summarize the chapter’s essential ideas. Remember the React Native Bridge: it is the communication layer between JavaScript and native platform code, enabling cross-language calls and event flow. A Native Module is native code you expose to JavaScript — on Android this often means a Kotlin or Java class that extends ReactContextBaseJavaModule and exposes methods with @ReactMethod. PermissionsAndroid is a built-in React Native A P I for requesting Android runtime permissions from JavaScript. Each of these concepts underpins how device features become available in a React Native app. Knowing these basics helps you evaluate when to use built-ins, adopt a library, or implement a custom module. Keep these definitions handy as you implement permission flows and device integrations. Key Concepts — Part 1 means bridge, native modules, and permissionsandroid are the foundational concepts enabling js to interact with native device features.. In practical terms, what to remember from this chapter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Bridge, Native Modules, and PermissionsAndroid are the foundational concepts enabling JS to interact with native device features.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Key Concepts
React Native Bridge
Communication channel between JavaScript and native code enabling calls and events.
Native Module
Platform code exposed to JavaScript, typically a Kotlin/Java class on Android or Swift/Objective-C on iOS.
PermissionsAndroid
Android-specific API in React Native for runtime permission requests from JavaScript.
Summary

Use the bridge to access device features, prefer built-in modules and libraries, and fall back to custom native modules only when necessary.

screens.subtitle: Practical terms for integration and debugging

narration.text: These final concepts are practical reminders as you work through integrations. @ReactMethod is the annotation used in Android native modules to expose a method to JavaScript; use it for methods you want to call across the bridge. ReactContextBaseJavaModule is the base class on Android for creating native modules — subclass it and implement getName to identify your module. AndroidManifest. xml must include any permissions or components your native code requires; declaring permissions there is required but you must also request runtime permission for dangerous actions. These terms map directly to the actions you will perform: annotate methods you expose, subclass the correct base class, and declare required permissions. Keep these items in mind while implementing and testing so your integrations are discoverable, callable, and compliant with platform rules.
